newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan lifts pork export ban, but requires permit.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan lifts pork export ban, but requires permit.

text.p: Taiwan said on Thursday it had lifted an export ban on pork, launched on March 20 due to an outbreak of a deadly hog disease, but officials said exporters must obtain permits from importing countries in advance.
"The pork export ban has been lifted at the Council of Agriculture's request, with immediate effect," an official at the Board of Foreign Trade told Reuters by telephone.
Agriculture council officials said exporters must first obtain permits from importing countries.
"We will no longer forbid pork exporters to export, but other countries must decide if they want to allow Taiwan's pork to enter," agriculture council official Chen Chung-jan said.
"No one has expressed interests to buy Taiwan pork so far and we don't expect to see any pork exports soon," Chen added.
The lifting of the pork export ban opens the door for other nations that also have the hog foot-and-mouth disease to import Taiwanese pork, another Council of Agriculture official said.
Taiwan on March 20 banned pork exports and ordered a mass slaughter and inoculation drive after confirming an outbreak of foot and mouth disease at nine hog farms.
The airborne virus has been detected on 3,422 of Taiwan's 25,000 hog farms, with officials projecting that 2.86 million of the island's 14 million pigs would have to be destroyed.
Farmers and soldiers were slaughtering all hogs -- healthy or otherwise -- at farms hit by the virus, while all cloven-hoofed livestock were being vaccinated at healthy farms.
Japan and South Korea have explicitly banned pork imports from Taiwan. The Philippines has forbidden imports of meat from any cloven-hoofed animal in Taiwan.
Taiwan has targetted 13 overseas markets, including Vietnam, Malaysia, Italy and Britain, as potential importers in an attempt to reduce local inventories and boost slumping prices.
Chen said countries that have no foot and mouth disease among their animals or have concerns about Taiwan's epidemic were likely to maintain their ban on Taiwan's pork.
Analysts say the epidemic could shave as much as one percentage point off Taiwan's gross domestic product growth in 1997, a major setback to its hard-won economic recovery.
